guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Where follow-up is incomplete, explain why the unobserved outcomes plausibly could or could not make an important difference to the approved estimate, rather than citing a small percentage alone. Relate the reported extent to the outcome event scale or variability and any known follow-up timing or reasons; retain what is unknown. For time-to-event estimates, event counts contextualize scale but do not by themselves mathematically bound the hazard ratio or its interval. A calibrated probable judgment can rest on nearly complete outcome accounting without exact censoring times or a formal sensitivity analysis. Missing reasons or timing alone do not require no_information; judge whether available circumstances support a reasonable inference.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.

Methods
Study design and participants
AWARD-10 was a 24-week, randomised, phase 3b,
double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled superiority
study done at 40 clinical sites in Austria, Czech Republic,
Germany, Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Spain, and the USA.
The study was completed in accordance with the
Declaration of Helsinki, the Council for International
Organisations of Medical Sciences International Ethical
Guidelines, and the International Conference on
Harmonisation Good Clinical Practices Guidelines. The
protocol was approved by local institutional review
boards. All patients provided written informed consent.
Eligible adult patients (≥18 years) had inadequately
controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c concentration ≥7∙0%
[53 mmol/mol] and ≤9∙5% [80 mmol/mol]), a BMI of
45 kg/m2 or less, and had been taking a commercially
available SGLT2 inhibitor with or without metformin
(≥1500 mg/day, as tolerated) for at least 3 months. We
excluded patients with type 1 diabetes; patients who used
any other glucose-lowering drugs (apart from an SGLT2
inhibitor and metformin) 3 months before study entry or
between study entry and randomisation; and patients with
a serum calcitonin concentration of 20 pg/mL or higher, a
history of pancreatitis, an episode of ketoacidosis or
hyperosmolar state or coma, a recent cardiovascular event,
or active cancer.
Randomisation and masking
Patients were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to subcutaneous
injection of dulaglutide 1∙5 mg, dulaglutide 0∙75 mg, or
placebo (all once weekly), stratified for baseline HbA1c
concentration, metformin use, and dose of SGLT2
inhibitor (low vs high). Low-dose SGLT2 inhibitor was
defined as the lowest dose approved at the time of trial
initiation in any of the participating countries
(canagliflozin 100 mg, dapagliflozin 5 mg, empagliflozin
10 mg) and high dose was defined as any dose greater
than the low dose. Stratification was intended to mitigate
baseline heterogeneity between treatment groups.
Randomisation was done by site personnel who
accessed the sponsor's interactive web-response system.
The system assigned cartons of double-blind study drug
for each patient using a computer-generated random
sequence. Site personnel were to confirm that they had
located the correct cartons by entering a confirmation
number found on the carton label into the system.
Procedures
A dose stabilisation period of up to 12 weeks between
screening and randomisation was permitted to allow
dose adjustments of SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, or
both-for example, when doses were lower than those
required according to the study design, or if a dose
reduction was required to comply with local regulatory
requirements (eg, decrease in estimated glomerular
filtration [eGFR]). Patients continued treatment with the
SGLT2 inhibitor with or without metformin after
randomisation without changes, except when required
per country-specific label. No dose adjustments of
injectable study drug (dulaglutide or placebo) were
allowed after randomisation.
During the study, new guidelines were published for
the adjustment of metformin dosing in response to
reductions in eGFR.22,23 In alignment with these
guidelines, patients with subsequent reductions in eGFR
were permitted to continue metformin treatment, with
appropriate dosing adjustment, within the eGFR range
of 31-45 mL/min per m2, with discontinuation of
metformin at an eGFR of 30 mL/min per m2 or less.
Compliance with study drug (dulaglutide or placebo)
was determined by review of the patient diary and return
of unused study drug at every visit at 2 weeks, 4 weeks,
8 weeks, 12 weeks, 18 weeks, and 24 weeks after
randomisation. Patients were considered compliant if at
least 75% of study drug doses were administered at each
visit interval and for at least 75% of visits attended. Poorly
compliant patients received additional training and
instructions, as required. Every attempt was made to
keep patients in the trial irrespective of their adherence
to treatment with study drug to minimise the amount of
missing data and to enable assessment of study objectives
per the study protocol.24
Based on prespecified criteria (appendix), patients
who had severe persistent hyperglycaemia or hypo-
glycaemia between study visits were advised to contact
the investigative site. For patients needing rescue
therapy for severe persistent hyperglycaemia, other oral
antihyperglycaemic drugs or insulin (no GLP-1 receptor
agonists) could be added as per published standards of
practice.16,21 For repeated episodes of hypoglycaemia, the
metformin dose could be reduced, proceeding to
complete withdrawal, as deemed necessary by the
investigator. Continued risk of hypoglycaemia, despite
discontinuation of metformin, warranted dose reduction
or complete withdrawal of the SGLT2 inhibitor. Patients
were to continue injectable study drug in either case.
Outcomes
The primary objective was to test for superiority of
dulaglutide relative to placebo for change in HbA1c
concentration from baseline to 24 weeks. The key secondary
outcomes assessed at 24 weeks were the percentage of
patients achieving an HbA1c target concentration of less
than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol), change from baseline in
bodyweight, and change from baseline in fasting serum
glucose concentration. Additional secondary outcomes
assessed at 24 weeks were percentage of patients achieving
an HbA1c target concentration of 6∙5% (48 mmol/mol) or
less, six-point self-monitored plasma glucose profile, and
change from baseline in fasting glucagon concentration.

4|Dulaglutide as add-on therapy to SGLT2 inhibitors in patients
5|with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes (AWARD-10):
6|a 24-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
7|Bernhard Ludvik*, Juan P FrÍas* , Francisco J Tinahones, Julio Wainstein, Honghua Jiang, Kenneth E Robertson, Luis-Emilio García-Pérez,
8|D Bradley Woodward, Zvonko Milicevic
9|Summary
10|Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2)
11|inhibitors improve glycaemic control and reduce bodyweight in patients with type 2 diabetes through different
12|mechanisms. We assessed the safety and efficacy of the addition of the once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist dulaglutide
13|to the ongoing treatment regimen in patients whose diabetes is inadequately controlled with SGLT2 inhibitors, with
14|or without metformin.
15|Methods AWARD-10 was a phase 3b, double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled, 24-week study done at 40 clinical
16|sites in Austria, Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Spain, and the USA. Eligible adult patients
17|(≥18 years) with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c concentration ≥7∙0% [53 mmol/mol] and
18|≤9∙5% [80 mmol/mol]), a BMI of 45 kg/m2 or less, and taking stable doses (>3 months) of an SGLT2 inhibitor (with
19|or without metformin) were randomly assigned (1:1:1) via an interactive web-response system to subcutaneous
20|injections of either dulaglutide 1∙5 mg, dulaglutide 0∙75 mg, or placebo once per week for 24 weeks. Patients and
21|investigators were masked to dulaglutide and placebo assignment, and those assessing outcomes were masked to
22|study drug assignment. The primary objective was to test for the superiority of dulaglutide (1∙5 mg or 0∙75 mg)
23|versus placebo for change in HbA1c concentration from baseline at 24 weeks. All analyses were done in the intention-
24|to-treat population, defined as all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of study drug. This study
25|is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT02597049.
26|Findings Between Dec 7, 2015, and Feb 3, 2017, 424 patients were randomly assigned to dulaglutide 1∙5 mg (n=142),
27|dulaglutide 0∙75 mg (n=142), and placebo (n=140). One patient in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group was excluded from the
28|analysis because they did not receive any dose of the study drug. The reduction in HbA1c concentration at 24 weeks was
29|larger in patients receiving dulaglutide (least squares mean [LSM] for dulaglutide 1∙5 mg -1∙34% [SE 0∙06] or
30|-14∙7 mmol/mol [0∙6]; dulaglutide 0∙75 mg -1∙21% [0∙06] or -13∙2 mmol/mol [0∙6]) than in patients receiving placebo
31|(-0∙54% [0∙06] or -5∙9 mmol/mol [0∙6]; p<0∙0001 for both groups vs placebo). The LSM differences were -0∙79% (95% CI
32|-0∙97 to -0∙61) or -8∙6 mmol/mol (-10∙6 to -6∙7) for dulaglutide 1∙5 mg and -0∙66% (-0∙84 to -0∙49) or -7∙2 mmol/mol
33|(-9∙2 to -5∙4) for dulaglutide 0∙75 mg (p<0∙0001 for both). Serious adverse events were reported for five (4%) patients in
34|the dulaglutide 1∙5 mg group, three (2%) patients in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group, and five (4%) patients in the placebo
35|group. Treatment-emergent adverse events were more common in patients treated with dulaglutide than in patients who
36|received placebo, mainly because of an increased incidence of gastrointestinal adverse events. Nausea (21 [15%] patients
37|in the dulaglutide 1∙5 mg group vs seven [5%] in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group vs five [4%] in the placebo group),
38|diarrhoea (eight [6%] vs 14 [10%] vs four [3%]), and vomiting (five [4%] vs four [3%] vs one [1%]) were more common with
39|dulaglutide than with placebo. One episode of severe hypoglycaemia was reported in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group.
40|Two (1%) patients receiving dulaglutide 1∙5 mg died, but these deaths were not considered to be related to study drug;
41|no deaths occurred in the other groups.
42|Interpretation Dulaglutide as add-on treatment to SGLT2 inhibitors (with or without metformin) resulted in
43|significant and clinically relevant improvements in glycaemic control, with acceptable tolerability that is consistent
44|with the established safety profile of dulaglutide.

86|Introduction
87|The use of pharmacological drugs as an addition to
88|lifestyle measures is the cornerstone of type 2 diabetes
89|treatment, and most patients need one or more
90|glucose-lowering drugs to achieve glycaemic control
91|targets. The rational use of these medications is based on
92|their stepwise initiation, wherein a new medication class
93|is added to the previously introduced medication class to
94|optimise the efficacy of the treatment regimen while
95|reducing the risk of side-effects.1 With combination
96|regimens, it is of special interest to investigate the effects
97|of concomitant use of drugs that have complementary

4|actions on the organs and tissues involved in the
5|regulation of carbohydrate metabolism or that might
6|have additive beneficial effects on the risk of
7|macrovascular and microvascular complications. The
8|combination of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor
9|agonists and sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2)
10|inhibitors is of particular relevance in this regard because
11|some drugs from these classes have been associated with
12|cardiovascular risk reduction in comparison with the
13|standard-of-care regimens. 2-4
14|GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors lower
15|plasma glucose concentrations, reduce bodyweight, and
16|bring about other clinically relevant outcomes through
17|different mechanism of actions. GLP-1 receptor agonists
18|enhance insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner,
19|inhibit glucagon secretion,5-15 slow gastric emptying
20|(especially with short-acting drugs), and suppress
21|appetite.16 Pharmacological inhibition of SGLT2 with
22|SGLT2 inhibitors promotes urinary glucose excretion and
23|indirectly increases glucagon concentration.17-19 These
24|complementary mechanisms of action suggest that the
25|combination of drugs from these two classes could have
26|additive effects on clinically important outcomes,
27|including glycaemic control, bodyweight, and blood
28|pressure.
29|Combination therapy with SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1
30|receptor agonists was not tested during the initial
31|clinical development of SGLT2 inhibitor drugs. In the
32|DURATION-8 trial,20 Frías and colleagues reported that
33|simultaneous initiation of drugs from these two classes
34|(exenatide once weekly plus dapagliflozin) improved
35|glycaemic control compared with each drug alone and
36|was well tolerated. To the best of our knowledge, the
37|stepwise initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonist in patients
38|receiving stable SGLT2 inhibitor therapy has never been
39|tested. The 24-week Assessment of Weekly AdministRation
40|of LY2189265 (dulaglutide) in Diabetes-10 (AWARD-10)
41|study was designed to assess the efficacy and safety of
42|dulaglutide (1∙5 mg or 0∙75 mg once weekly) when added
43|to stable doses of an SGLT2 inhibitor (with or without
44|metformin) in patients with inadequately controlled
45|type 2 diabetes. The design of the AWARD-10 study design
46|is in line with the American Diabetes Association (ADA)
47|and European Association for the Study of Diabetes
48|(EASD) recommendation1,16,21 of a step-wise treatment
49|strategy (add-on to existing therapy) as type 2 diabetes
50|Research in context
51|Evidence before this study
52|We searched PubMed on July 18, 2017, using the terms
53|"liraglutide", "exenatide", "albiglutide", "lixisenatide", and
54|"empagliflozin", "dapagliflozin", "canagliflozin", and
55|"randomised controlled trial" and "type 2 diabetes", with no
56|date or trial duration restrictions. Non-English language
57|references were excluded. The search returned
58|179 publications, two of which included clinical data for the
59|combination of a glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) receptor
60|agonists and sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2)
61|inhibitor in a controlled clinical study. Fulcher and colleagues
62|reported a post-hoc analysis of the CANVAS trial, in which
63|canagliflozin was added to background GLP-1 receptor agonist
64|therapy, with difference versus placebo reported at 18 weeks.
65|95 patients were included in the analysis. Placebo-subtracted
66|reductions in HbA1c for canagliflozin 100 mg and 300 mg were
67|-1·00% (95% CI -1·35 to -0·65) and -1·06% (-1·43 to -0·69),
68|respectively, for patients on GLP-1 receptor agonist
69|background therapy. Reductions in bodyweight, plasma
70|glucose, and blood pressure were also reported. Frías and
71|colleagues reported results from a 28-week, phase 3,
72|multicentre, double-blind, randomised, active-controlled
73|clinical trial (DURATION-8), in which 231 patients received
74|exenatide once weekly plus dapagliflozin, 231 received
75|exenatide once weekly alone, and 233 received dapagliflozin
76|alone. Reductions in HbA1c for exenatide plus dapagliflozin
77|were significantly greater from baseline to week 28 compared
78|with exenatide alone (-0·4% [95% CI -0·6 to -0·1]; p=0·004)
79|or dapagliflozin alone (-0·6% [-0·8 to -0·3]; p<0·001).
80|Reductions in bodyweight, plasma glucose, and systolic blood
81|pressure were also greater for exenatide plus dapagliflozin than
82|for other treatments.
83|Added value of this study
84|To our knowledge, there are no other reports of phase 3,
85|randomised, controlled clinical trials wherein a GLP-1 receptor
86|agonist has been added to ongoing treatment with stable
87|doses of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with inadequately
88|controlled type 2 diabetes. In DURATION-8, the GLP-1 receptor
89|agonist (exenatide once weekly) was initiated at the same time
90|as the SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), whereas in our study
91|(AWARD-10), we assessed a stepwise treatment strategy as
92|recommended by the American Diabetes Association and the
93|European Association for the Study of Diabetes. Additionally,
94|compared with DURATION-8, in which dapagliflozin was
95|specifically assessed, our study permitted the use of any
96|approved SGLT2 inhibitor and included patients with a lower
97|range of mean baseline HbA1c concentrations who needed a
98|new intervention because the target HbA1c concentration of
99|less than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol) had not been achieved.
100|Implications from all the available evidence
101|Our findings show that, compared with placebo, dulaglutide
102|given as add-on treatment to any of the three available SGLT2
103|inhibitors (with or without metformin) results in significant
104|and clinically relevant improvements in glycaemic control and
105|other outcomes, with acceptable tolerability that is consistent
106|with the established safety profile of dulaglutide. These
107|findings further inform the use of a once weekly GLP-1
108|receptor agonist in combination with SGLT2 inhibitors in
109|patients with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes.

6|Methods
7|Study design and participants
8|AWARD-10 was a 24-week, randomised, phase 3b,
9|double-blind, parallel-arm, placebo-controlled superiority
10|study done at 40 clinical sites in Austria, Czech Republic,
11|Germany, Hungary, Israel, Mexico, Spain, and the USA.
12|The study was completed in accordance with the
13|Declaration of Helsinki, the Council for International
14|Organisations of Medical Sciences International Ethical
15|Guidelines, and the International Conference on
16|Harmonisation Good Clinical Practices Guidelines. The
17|protocol was approved by local institutional review
18|boards. All patients provided written informed consent.
19|Eligible adult patients (≥18 years) had inadequately
20|controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c concentration ≥7∙0%
21|[53 mmol/mol] and ≤9∙5% [80 mmol/mol]), a BMI of
22|45 kg/m2 or less, and had been taking a commercially
23|available SGLT2 inhibitor with or without metformin
24|(≥1500 mg/day, as tolerated) for at least 3 months. We
25|excluded patients with type 1 diabetes; patients who used
26|any other glucose-lowering drugs (apart from an SGLT2
27|inhibitor and metformin) 3 months before study entry or
28|between study entry and randomisation; and patients with
29|a serum calcitonin concentration of 20 pg/mL or higher, a
30|history of pancreatitis, an episode of ketoacidosis or
31|hyperosmolar state or coma, a recent cardiovascular event,
32|or active cancer.
33|Randomisation and masking
34|Patients were randomly assigned (1:1:1) to subcutaneous
35|injection of dulaglutide 1∙5 mg, dulaglutide 0∙75 mg, or
36|placebo (all once weekly), stratified for baseline HbA1c
37|concentration, metformin use, and dose of SGLT2
38|inhibitor (low vs high). Low-dose SGLT2 inhibitor was
39|defined as the lowest dose approved at the time of trial
40|initiation in any of the participating countries
41|(canagliflozin 100 mg, dapagliflozin 5 mg, empagliflozin
42|10 mg) and high dose was defined as any dose greater
43|than the low dose. Stratification was intended to mitigate
44|baseline heterogeneity between treatment groups.
45|Randomisation was done by site personnel who
46|accessed the sponsor's interactive web-response system.
47|The system assigned cartons of double-blind study drug
48|for each patient using a computer-generated random
49|sequence. Site personnel were to confirm that they had
50|located the correct cartons by entering a confirmation
51|number found on the carton label into the system.
52|Procedures
53|A dose stabilisation period of up to 12 weeks between
54|screening and randomisation was permitted to allow
55|dose adjustments of SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin, or
56|both-for example, when doses were lower than those
57|required according to the study design, or if a dose
58|reduction was required to comply with local regulatory
59|requirements (eg, decrease in estimated glomerular
60|filtration [eGFR]). Patients continued treatment with the
61|SGLT2 inhibitor with or without metformin after
62|randomisation without changes, except when required
63|per country-specific label. No dose adjustments of
64|injectable study drug (dulaglutide or placebo) were
65|allowed after randomisation.
66|During the study, new guidelines were published for
67|the adjustment of metformin dosing in response to
68|reductions in eGFR.22,23 In alignment with these
69|guidelines, patients with subsequent reductions in eGFR
70|were permitted to continue metformin treatment, with
71|appropriate dosing adjustment, within the eGFR range
72|of 31-45 mL/min per m2, with discontinuation of
73|metformin at an eGFR of 30 mL/min per m2 or less.
74|Compliance with study drug (dulaglutide or placebo)
75|was determined by review of the patient diary and return
76|of unused study drug at every visit at 2 weeks, 4 weeks,
77|8 weeks, 12 weeks, 18 weeks, and 24 weeks after
78|randomisation. Patients were considered compliant if at
79|least 75% of study drug doses were administered at each
80|visit interval and for at least 75% of visits attended. Poorly
81|compliant patients received additional training and
82|instructions, as required. Every attempt was made to
83|keep patients in the trial irrespective of their adherence
84|to treatment with study drug to minimise the amount of
85|missing data and to enable assessment of study objectives
86|per the study protocol.24
87|Based on prespecified criteria (appendix), patients
88|who had severe persistent hyperglycaemia or hypo-
89|glycaemia between study visits were advised to contact
90|the investigative site. For patients needing rescue
91|therapy for severe persistent hyperglycaemia, other oral
92|antihyperglycaemic drugs or insulin (no GLP-1 receptor
93|agonists) could be added as per published standards of
94|practice.16,21 For repeated episodes of hypoglycaemia, the
95|metformin dose could be reduced, proceeding to
96|complete withdrawal, as deemed necessary by the
97|investigator. Continued risk of hypoglycaemia, despite
98|discontinuation of metformin, warranted dose reduction
99|or complete withdrawal of the SGLT2 inhibitor. Patients
100|were to continue injectable study drug in either case.
101|Outcomes
102|The primary objective was to test for superiority of
103|dulaglutide relative to placebo for change in HbA1c
104|concentration from baseline to 24 weeks. The key secondary
105|outcomes assessed at 24 weeks were the percentage of
106|patients achieving an HbA1c target concentration of less
107|than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol), change from baseline in
108|bodyweight, and change from baseline in fasting serum
109|glucose concentration. Additional secondary outcomes
110|assessed at 24 weeks were percentage of patients achieving
111|an HbA1c target concentration of 6∙5% (48 mmol/mol) or
112|less, six-point self-monitored plasma glucose profile, and
113|change from baseline in fasting glucagon concentration.

12|Adverse events, laboratory parameters, vital signs, and
13|electrocardiograms were assessed for safety. Adverse
14|events of special interest included hypoglycaemia,
15|hyperglycaemia, pancreatitis (abdominal pain, pancreatic
16|enzymes), thyroid safety (serum calcitonin, C-cell
17|hyperplasia, neoplasms), cardiovascular events, renal
18|events, allergic or hypersensitivity reactions, hypotension,
19|urogenital infections, diabetic ketoacidosis, and poten
20|tially important gastrointestinal adverse events, such as
21|cholelithiasis or appendicitis. Cases of pancreatitis or
22|cardiovascular events (fatal or non-fatal) were confirmed
23|by independent adjudication. Laboratory measurements
24|were done centrally at time of screening, at time of
25|randomisation, and at 24 weeks (final endpoint) via a
26|central laboratory. A data safety monitoring board was
27|not used in this study; however, masked trial-level safety
28|reviews were done by the study funder.
29|Hypoglycaemia rate and incidence were recorded as
30|described by Seaquist and colleagues25 and documented
31|as symptomatic, asymptomatic, probable symptomatic,
32|severe, nocturnal, and total. Additional details about
33|hypoglycaemia are reported in the appendix.
34|Statistical analysis
35|We estimated that 120 completers per treatment group
36|would provide 90% power to detect superiority of
37|dulaglutide 1∙5 mg or 0∙75 mg versus placebo in change
38|in mean HbA1c concentration from baseline to 24 weeks.
39|An SD of 1∙2% (13∙1 mmol/mol), a difference between
40|dulaglutide and placebo of 0∙55% (6∙0 mmol/mol), and
41|a 15% dropout rate were assumed; and a two-sided
42|significance level of 0∙025 was used in this power
43|calculation.26

18|Results
19|Between Dec 7, 2015, and Feb 3, 2017, 424 patients were
20|randomly assigned to receive dulaglutide 1∙5 mg (n=142),
21|dulaglutide 0∙75 mg (n=142), or placebo (n=140; figure 1).
22|Seven (5%) patients in the dulaglutide 1∙5 mg group,
23|five (4%) patients in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg, and
24|three (2%) patients in the placebo group discontinued the
25|study early (figure 1). The most frequent reasons for study
26|discontinuation were adverse events, loss to follow-up,
27|and withdrawal by the patient. Baseline characteristics
28|were similar between treatment groups (table 1). The
29|duration of SGLT2 inhibitor and metformin treatment at
30|time of screening and the mean SGLT2 inhibitor doses at
31|baseline are summarised in the appendix. Across all
32|treatment groups, most patients had taken an SGLT2
33|inhibitor for 3-6 months; high-dose dapagliflozin (about
34|10 mg/day) and low-dose empagliflozin (10 mg/day) were
35|the most commonly used SGLT2 inhibitors at screening
36|and study end. The mean doses of the SGLT2 inhibitors
37|and metformin were stable from baseline to study end.
38|15 patients (two in the dulaglutide 1·5 mg group, three in
39|the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group, and ten in the placebo
40|group) received rescue therapy for hyperglycaemia or an
41|adverse event (appendix). Additionally, eight patients
42|(three in the dulaglutide 1∙5 mg group, four in the
43|dulaglutide 0∙75 mg group, and one in the placebo group)
44|discontinued study drug early and were retained in the
45|study. One patient in the dulaglutide 0∙75 mg did not
46|receive any doses of study drug and was therefore excluded
47|from analysis in the intention-to-treat population.
48|Changes in HbA1c concentration from baseline to
49|24 weeks were larger with both dulaglutide doses than
50|with placebo (p<0∙0001; figure 2A).
51|The proportions of patients who achieved the HbA1c
52|target concentrations of less than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol)
53|and 6∙5% (48 mmol/mol) or less at 24 weeks was also
54|larger in the dulaglutide groups than in the placebo
55|group (p<0∙0001; figure 2B).
56|Reduction in bodyweight from baseline to 24 weeks
57|was greater with dulaglutide 1∙5 mg than with placebo

9|Because of their relatively recent regulatory approvals,
10|combination use of GLP-1 receptor agonists with SGLT2
11|inhibitors is still not common practice, despite potential
12|advantages over other combinations commonly used to
13|treat patients with type 2 diabetes. In the AWARD-10 trial,
14|addition of once-weekly dulaglutide to ongoing treatment
15|with an SGLT2 inhibitor (with or without metformin)
16|resulted in significant and clinically relevant improvement
17|in HbA1c concentration as compared with placebo. This
18|regimen also resulted in greater reduction of bodyweight
19|with dulaglutide 1∙5 mg. Tolerability of dulaglutide was
20|consistent with its known profile when used to treat
21|patients with type 2 diabetes.26 Improvements in glycaemic
22|control were observed with limited risk of hypoglycaemia
23|and without unexpected adverse events. Although the
24|design of AWARD-10 differed from that of DURATION-8,20
25|another randomised trial of GLP-1 receptor agonist and
26|SGLT2 inhibitor co-administration, the results of these
27|two trials suggest multiple potential benefits of this
28|combination in patients with type 2 diabetes.
29|The current recommended approach to improve
30|glycaemic control while minimising side-effects in the
31|treatment of type 2 diabetes is to individualise therapy to
32|satisfy patient needs, using a clinical strategy that is
33|based on stepwise addition of different classes of glucose-
34|lowering drugs.16,21 Combination therapy with GLP-1
35|receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors has received
36|particular interest because these drug classes have
37|complementary effects with respect to glycaemic control.
38|Additionally, findings from several completed studies
39|suggest that drugs from both classes can reduce the risk
40|of cardiovascular events in people at high cardiovascular
41|risk, potentially in part because of effects on bodyweight
42|and blood pressure.2,3,28 Data describing the effect of
43|adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist to ongoing SGLT2
44|inhibitor treatment regimens are limited. In one large-
45|scale,
46|randomised
47|clinical
48|trial
49|(DURATION-8),20
50|simultaneous initiation of a GLP-1 receptor agonist
51|(exenatide once weekly) and an SGLT2 inhibitor
52|(dapagliflozin) improved glycaemic control, bodyweight,
53|and systolic blood pressure compared with either drug
54|alone in patients with inadequately controlled type 2
55|diabetes.20 Similar results were observed when the SGLT2
56|inhibitor canagliflozin was added to ongoing therapy
57|with a GLP-1 analogue in the the long-term CVOT
58|CANVAS study.29 Data from retrospective observational
59|studies suggest that GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2
60|inhibitors are used together off-label in clinical settings
61|for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.30,31
62|We used a study design consistent with the recom
63|mendations by the ADA and EASD for the treatment of
64|patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for step-
65|wise introduction of glucose-lowering drugs from
66|different classes. The addition of dulaglutide to ongoing
67|SGLT2 inhibitor treatment (with or without metformin)
68|resulted in clinically relevant glucose-lowering effects, as
69|measured by change from baseline in HbA1c concentration
70|at 24 weeks, and a substantial increase in number of
71|patients reaching the standard treatment target of an
72|HbA1c concentration less than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol). This
73|outcome suggests that the glucose-lowering efficacy of
74|dulaglutide is preserved when initiated in patients treated
75|with SGLT2 inhibitors under conditions of inadequate
76|glycaemic control. Both dulaglutide doses reduced all
77|plasma glucose values from the six-point daily self-
78|monitored plasma glucose profiles versus placebo,
79|suggesting that the reduction in HbA1c concentration is
80|achieved through improvements in fasting, preprandial,
81|and postprandial plasma glucose control. This observation
82|is consistent with changes in the daily self-monitored
83|plasma glucose profile in patients treated with dulaglutide
84|in previous studies.5-13 The improvement in glucose
85|control was not associated with an increase in the risk of
86|hypoglycaemia because only one episode of severe
87|hypoglycaemia was reported during this trial, confirming
88|the previous observation of a very low incidence of
89|hypoglycaemia with dulaglutide in combination with
90|non-secretagogues. In the case of hypoglycaemia episodes,
91|the trial design required that patients stop metformin
92|first, since the objective of the trial was to study dulaglutide
93|plus SGLT2 inhibitors in combination. In the real clinical
94|situation, since all three drug classes that patients received
95|are non-secretagogues, any of them could be discontinued
96|to mitigate the risk of new events, taking into account
97|patients' preference, adherence, and clinical response to
98|each of these medications.
99|Clinically relevant improvement in daily and long-term
100|glucose control with combined use of dulaglutide and
101|SGLT2 inhibitors is important in the context of the
102|differences
103|in
104|mechanisms
105|of
106|actions
107|between
108|GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors-
109|enhancement of insulin secretion and glucagon
110|suppression with GLP-1 receptor agonists versus
111|increased urinary glucose excretion and glucagon
112|stimulation with SGLT2 inhibitors. Understanding the
113|effect on glucagon was of special interest in this study
114|because treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors has been
115|shown to increase glucagon concentrations,17-19 potentially
116|interfering with glucagon-lowering actions of GLP-1
117|receptor agonists. Importantly, both dulaglutide doses
118|suppressed serum glucagon secretion, with dulaglutide
119|1∙5 mg achieving a significantly greater reduction from
120|baseline versus placebo, consistent with the reductions
121|in fasting glucagon concentration of similar magnitude
122|reported in other studies of dulaglutide.7,11 The preserved
123|effect of dulaglutide on glucagon when added to SGLT2
124|inhibitor treatment might be an important contributor to
125|the overall glucose-lowering potency in this patient

4|population. This preserved effect is not seen with
5|dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors or liraglutide
6|when added to treatment with SGLT2 inhibitors since
7|mean glucagon concentrations remained unchanged.32,33
8|This finding is potentially due to the lower potency of
9|DPP-4 inhibitors and liraglutide compared with
10|dulaglutide in the suppression of glucagon secretion.
11|The reduction in HbA1c and bodyweight with dulaglutide
12|1∙5 mg in our study (about 1 kg of additional decrease
13|vs placebo) was statistically significant in all analyses
14|apart from the mixed-model for repeated measures
15|without data collected after the initiation of rescue
16|intervention. The estimated absolute reduction in
17|bodyweight was 3∙1 kg in the dulaglutide 1∙5 mg group in
18|AWARD-10; in the DURATION-8 trial, simultaneous
19|introduction of exenatide once weekly and dapagliflozin
20|resulted in a bodyweight reduction of 3∙4 kg.20
21|It is noteworthy that the reduction in HbA1c concentration
22|and bodyweight of patients assigned to placebo in
23|AWARD-10 was larger than expected. One possible reason
24|could be related to the late introduction of SGLT2 inhibitor
25|therapy in many patients (3-6 months before study entry).
26|In other words, continuous decrease in HbA1c and
27|bodyweight in the placebo group after randomisation
28|might suggest that the bodyweight-lowering action of
29|recently introduced SGLT2 inhibitors was ongoing during
30|the treatment period. However, we could not confirm this
31|hypothesis in our assessment of the effect on HbA1c and
32|bodyweight by duration of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. We
33|have also ruled out a potential effect of rescue interventions
34|that patients received during the treatment period. It is
35|unlikely that metformin therapy had a role since this drug
36|was introduced on average more than 2 years before the
37|study, and doses were stable and unchanged during the
38|trial. Finally, it is not uncommon to see similar decreases
39|in bodyweight and HbA1c concentration without any clear
40|reason (ie, study effect) in clinical trials that include
41|patients with type 2 diabetes.18,34,35 Although these changes
42|in bodyweight and HbA1c concentration over time in the
43|placebo group might have affected the precise estimate of
44|the contribution of dulaglutide to these outcomes, the
45|trends reported for these measures in the placebo group
46|did not affect our conclusions derived from the study
47|results.
48|The effect of dulaglutide on glycaemic control, body
49|weight, and hypoglycaemia risk translated into a larger
50|proportion of patients treated with dulaglutide who
51|achieved the prespecified composite endpoint of an HbA1c
52|concentration less than 7∙0% (53 mmol/mol) without
53|bodyweight gain and without documented symptomatic
54|hypoglycaemia at 24 weeks versus placebo. Composite
55|endpoints are an important tool for assessing how many
56|patients can reach their glycaemic goals without signifi
57|cant patient-relevant side-effects that are often an obstacle
58|in obtaining optimal glucose-lowering outcomes.
59|Overall, the safety findings were consistent with results
60|of previous studies of dulaglutide in patients with
61|type 2 diabetes, and no new safety concerns were identified.
62|Similar proportions of patients in all three treatment
63|groups had treatment-emergent adverse events. There
64|were no cases of acute pancreatitis, C-cell hyperplasia, or
65|medullary thyroid cancer during the study. Few patients
66|reported one or more treatment-emergent adverse events
67|that were identified as possibly related to hypotension, a
68|potential concern when two classes of drugs, both of which
69|might cause blood pressure decrease, are combined. No
70|amputations, cases of diabetic ketoacidosis, or acute
71|kidney injury events were reported, and the overall number
72|of urogenital infections was lower than anticipated in a
73|group of patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors, possibly
74|because of a lower risk in chronically treated patients.
75|The decrease in systolic blood pressure was larger with
76|dulaglutide 1∙5 mg than with placebo, and the change in
77|diastolic blood pressure did not differ between treatment
78|groups. The reduction in systolic blood pressure was
79|consistent with that reported in previous dulaglutide
80|studies. Dulaglutide led to an additional decrease of
81|systolic blood pressure, beyond that observed in the
82|placebo group, suggesting an additive effect of the
83|combination regimen. The reduction in systolic blood
84|pressure, a major cardiovascular risk factor, is of
85|considerable relevance since drugs from the GLP-1
86|receptor agonist and SGLT2 inhibitor classes have been
87|shown to reduce cardiovascular risk in cardiovascular
88|outcome studies. For example, the GLP-1 receptor agonist
89|liraglutide2 and the SGLT2 inhibitors empagliflozin and
90|canagliflozin3,4 were shown to reduce the composite
91|endpoint of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial
92|infarction, or non-fatal stroke in patients at high
93|cardiovascular risk. In the DURATION-8 trial, Frías and
94|colleagues20 showed that concomitant therapy with
95|exenatide once weekly and dapagliflozin resulted in
96|greater improvements in cardiovascular risk factors,
97|including HbA1c, bodyweight, and systolic blood pressure,
98|than did the individual drugs alone, albeit in a population
99|of patients with HbA1c concentration greater than
100|8% (64 mmol/mol) and lower than 12% (108 mmol/mol).
101|In the present study, we have shown significantly greater
102|improvements in these cardiovascular risk factors
103|when dulaglutide 1·5 mg is added on to stable SGLT2
104|inhibitor therapy. The ongoing cardiovascular outcome
105|study (REWIND [NCT01394952]) will provide additional
106|information about the cardiovascular effects of dula
107|glutide in patients with type 2 diabetes.28
108|Limitations of this study include the relatively short
109|duration (24 weeks). A longer study might have provided
110|additional insight into the clinical relevance of concomitant
111|use of dulaglutide and SGLT2 inhibitors. However,
112|guidelines limit placebo-controlled trials to 6 months'
113|duration.36,37 The trial included patients with inadequate
114|glycaemic control, but with an HbA1c concentration of
115|9∙5% or less, treated with an SGLT2 inhibitor with or
116|without metformin (≥1500 mg per day, as tolerated). The
117|results can therefore not be generalised to patients who do

answers.justification: The approved Result is the centrally measured HbA1c change from baseline at 24 weeks for assignment to dulaglutide 1.5 mg or 0.75 mg versus placebo, retaining the randomized-population target despite the narrower reported ITT population (one randomized participant received no dose and was excluded). The report says 424 were randomized and the trial profile records 135/142, 137/142, and 137/140 as completing the study (409/424 overall); it reports only 15 early study discontinuations (7, 5, and 3), while eight who stopped study drug remained in the study. This supports nearly complete follow-up as a reasonable, calibrated inference, but completed-study counts are not direct counts of HbA1c measurements at 24 weeks, and analysis membership is not outcome availability. Thus probably yes rather than definitive yes; exact arm-specific observed/imputed HbA1c counts and participant-level endpoint ascertainment are not reported in the inspected material. The one excluded randomized participant and incomplete follow-up remain noted; the small overall fraction is judged unlikely to materially change this continuous-outcome estimate, without treating it as a universal threshold.
unknowns: Exact arm-specific observed HbA1c values at 24 weeks, imputed outcomes, and endpoint availability among the 15 who discontinued study are not reported.
The analysis excluded one randomized dulaglutide 0.75 mg participant who received no dose; this remains a scope difference from the all-randomized target.

counterevidence.implication: The trial profile records 15 participants discontinuing the study before 24 weeks, including losses to follow-up and withdrawals, and the reported ITT excludes one randomized participant; this prevents concluding complete ascertainment and leaves exact endpoint availability uncertain.
